sources.entry: Circuit Breaker (mentioned in the Release it! book)

summary.title: bliki: Circuit Breaker
summary.one_liner: A circuit breaker wraps remote calls, trips after repeated failures so calls fail fast without reaching the struggling supplier, and can self-reset via a half-open trial call.
keywords: how to stop calling a failing service
takeaways: Wrap remote calls in a breaker that counts failures and trips open past a threshold, returning an error without calling the supplier.
Add a half-open state with a reset timeout so the breaker makes a trial call and closes again if the supplier recovers.
Use a per-call timeout and run calls on a thread pool so the circuit trips when the pool is exhausted.
Log and monitor breaker state changes, and let operations staff trip or reset breakers.
Decide per operation how to handle a broken circuit, such as queuing the request or showing stale data.
summary.summary:
Martin Fowler explains the Circuit Breaker pattern, popularized by Michael Nygard's Release It!, for protecting systems from slow or failing remote calls that can cascade across services. He builds a simple Ruby breaker that counts timeouts and opens after a threshold, then extends it with a self-resetting half-open state that sends a trial call after a reset timeout. The article also covers thread pool and asynchronous queue variants, failure-rate thresholds, monitoring, and fallback handling, and ends with pointers to Netflix's Hystrix and other open-source implementations.</isummary>
